articles.title: The end of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers group

top_comments: This is true in every large company right now.The transformer based approach is seen as a highway to race down in terms of training and building better models with minimal organizational distractions allowed while every company puts its foot down on this highway. Exploratory research into other AI methods is highly discouraged for now and organizations are encouraging transformer based scale out and iteration as a top priority.As an example Meta literally fired it's previously head of AI who held views that transformers won't scale. He wanted to veer off the highway and heavily fund exploratory new types of models. They got someone willing to scale the current method out. Essentially the messaging it "Foot down, there's a straight highway ahead don't divert".I have the view this makes sense too. Current top models are mere (mere in big datacenter terms) trillions of parameters right now. We definitely haven't hit the ceiling and everyone's noticing "Hey this Opus 5.5 with the increased parameters seems much better than the last one". Well that's a trillion parameter model. We'll soon start hitting 10's of trillions and 100's of trillions of parameter models. Unless there's a ceiling which nobody expects they should keep scaling just as they have been. I really do agree that it'd be insane to veer off this highway with exploratory research at this particular point in time. Foot down, get to 10 trillion parameters, see if the scaling holds, if so off to 100 trillion parameters. If the scaling continues to hold we'll be asking the AI to do the exploratory research for us soon enough.

This refers specifically to "AI Frontiers", a research group within Microsoft Research that focuses on fundamental advances in AI. There is no end in sight to real AI frontiers.Perhaps "The End of Microsoft Research's AI Frontiers Group" would be a less ambiguous title.

It makes me sad because there are so many unexplored areas of AI research, even on text generation. Billions are invested in almost one idea, which very realistically isn't the most optimal way to do text generation, but a lot of companies are afraid of taking risks. I still wouldn't put $1b on JEPA but I prefer a world where we can try things like that.

articles.title: Claude Code's "Don't Ask Again" exposes passwords in 1,122 public GitHub files
articles.summary: Claude Code's "Don't Ask Again" exposes passwords in 1,122 public GitHub files

top_comments: Boris from the Claude Code team here. Historically Claude Code has not done secret scrubbing (there are many good tools for that), but we are looking into what we can do to prevent this.That said, a few thoughts:1. .claude/settings.local.json is meant to stay local. This is not a file you should check into source control. We automatically gitignore it when Claude creates the file, so in this case the files were manually created and checked in (docs: https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings)2. Permission rules are old hat. Everyone should be using auto mode instead. It is safer and also does not require manually maintaining finicky allow/deny lists. Auto mode is enabled by default and is included for free in all plans.3. Regardless of what agent you use, you should have secret scanning enabled. GitHub and other source control hosts offer it. There are many threat models that it protects against and you should absolutely use it if you can. (see https://github.com/security/plans)

Confusing headline. They scanned for repos where people had committed their .claude/ folder and local settings and then scanned those files for commands which contained keys or passwords.So pressing “Don’t Ask Again” by itself doesn’t expose passwords by itself. If you commit your local Claude settings and in those settings you have manually approved commands containing secrets directly in the command and then you publish the repo, that’s exposed.

I'm super paranoid about the level of access AI agents have. At the same time, I want them to take away the tedium of a bunch of tasks I'm required to do, and it sucks to have to micromanage them.The best solution I've been able to come up is using an ephemeral vm (on an isolated network) per task, using --dangerously-skip-permissions so it doesn't bother me. I couple that with an API proxy that lets me restrict the permissions it has to external services. So e.g. where a quickbooks API key gives the holder "god mode" access, the proxy lets the agent do certain read commands without confirmation, but all write endpoints except uploading receipts require confirmation on my phone before they'll be allowed to hit the quickbooks servers. I no longer need to trust that the agent will interpret my readonly wishes correctly.Tooting my own horn here, but this setup works incredibly well! I've been able to connect dozens of services safely where I absolutely do not trust giving raw, overpowered credentials or oauth integration to the agent directly. I actually just released the API proxy today at https://keycontain.com

articles.title: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?"
articles.summary: MaxxBench – "Nice DeepSWE score. But is it true?"

top_comments: This is a great example of how to test how well a benchmark score generalises. The first order approximation is not complicated: just vary a parameter and see how much the score changes.Which parameter to vary depends on the result of the test, but the MaxxBench route of varying the task spec seems like a good default, though not always the most informative.In one of my private benchmarks I realised many of the less capable models didn't fail because they submitted the wrong answer, but because they exceeded their budget for number of tool calls they were allowed. The more capable models never got close to the tool call limit because they tended toward combining tool calls (e.g. chaining multiple shell commands in one Bash tool call).Was my benchmark actually measuring ability to combine tool calls rather than reasoning ability on the problem at hand? Well, easy enough to find out: re-run under a different tool call budget and see how much the scores change.(Next problem: is ability to combine tool calls a useful thing to measure, i.e. should it confer an advantage in the benchmark? It could be if it is a sign of planning multiple steps ahead.)

Academically a - very - interesting article, which confirms my ongoing suspicion of LLM Benchmarks in general ( probably why I like it so much). Another thing that caught my eye is DeepSWE having a bunch of bugs in them. The more I learn about these benchmarks the more sceptical I become. I would expect such a prolific benchmark to have these bugs ironed out by now.The practical takeaway, however, seems to be an interesting "don't use max mode". The passage about deepseeks weird API behavior dropping to pretty much zero the moment you used high says a lot.Also, personally, even though Opus is clearly so much ahead of the Open Source models after the changes, I think the adjusted score is still very much competitive. I see other commenters using this as proof to justify why their opinions of the open source models - but a drop from 74% to ~50% is, while a big drop, still about a ~50% pass rate afterwards. That's far from useless for coding, especially since DeepSWE seems to be such a difficult benchmark. It simply seems to more accurately reflect the capabilities of these models.All in all, I'd love to see more of such articles, and will probably keep an eye on this one - if they continue "benchmarking" these models this way.

The big trend in that graph is that smaller models collapse the most. Everything with "-flash" in the name, plus OpenAI Luna.Look at GPT 5.6-Sol vs. GPT 5.6-Luna in particular.(The GLM pair shouldn't be expected follow this pattern, because they're misnamed: GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-flash are distinct lineages. The -flash is an early release of a new pretrain on a new architecture).If this *is* the main factor, I'd expect Kimi K3.1 and Gemini Carbon would also do well on this test (unlike Gemini-flash); while Haiku 6 would collapse (breaking the trend of the other recent Claude models). It's a falsifiable prediction.

articles.title: Show HN: Coldframe, a honeypot that poses as a supermarket fridge controller
articles.summary: I built Coldframe, a honeypot that pretends to be a supermarket refrigeration controller. Inspired by the events on industrial fridge installations in the past weeks, I wanted to see what people would try against a convincing fake.To learn more about this I built a honeypot that resembled perfectly the Danfoss AK-SM 800A and Dixell XWEB interfaces. Both of them are recognized on Shodan as real ones (an not as honeypots). It’s one Python file using only the standard library, and it builds on eppser/danfoss-ak-sm-decoy and public research by Synacktiv, Claroty and Ironhackers.Things that were fun to get right:- Matching real units. I used Shodan records of real devices to match header order, page titles, certificate fields and TLS versions. The Danfoss persona sends nginx headers in the same order as a real AK-SM 800A. The Dixell persona sends no Server header and pads its page to exactly 8,202 bytes.- Recognising exploit attempts. It recognises CVE-2025-41450, the Danfoss “code of the day” login bypass, and records whether the submitted code is correct for today. It also tags attempts targeting three other Danfoss CVEs and the XWEB vulnerabilities.- Letting them in. Default logins open a fake store dashboard with defrost buttons, so you see the second move, not just the first. Nothing behind it is real.Two instances have been live for a day. So far they’ve only seen generic scanners and Shodan’s crawler, which is called refrigerator.census.shodan.io.Feedback welcome, especially from anyone who has seen these devices in the field!

top_comments: I would be very skeptical of anyone relying on Shodan data. At one point I was trying to write honeypots myself by replicating wifi cameras, but almost all the ones on the internet I found were honeypots of some sort, and the ones that weren't were already hacked and had their web pages replaced. In retrospect it would have probably been better to get a vulnerable device myself and probe it.If I were you, I would probably ensure that the fridges you used have residential or commercial (aka non-DC) IP addresses. Maybe Shodan uses this data for their "honeypot" label, my experience was some time ago so no idea though.

An extra insight, there was some news of 'blood banks' also being targetted. This is possibly a stronger (painful) target. It would demorelize people that are donors. https://www.independent.co.uk/tech/security/blood-hack-fridg...

One thing keeps coming back, (and it's the story of industries where security and patching is an afterthought).a supermarket has no security team. If a fridge controller needs patching, a VPN and a strong password to be safe, that work has to come from the vendor or installer by default. One would hope that all these come by default or as a feature on these devices. It could even be a selling feature and not part of an expensive maintenance contract. A supermarket manager cannot be expected to do this work.

I used to use ChatGPT/Claude in the TUI up until like 3 months ago, but my usage of LLMs has exploded - many sessions across many projects. I feel like I outgrew the TUI and now I'm using ChatGPT/Claude desktop. VS Code has become a code review tool and place where I manage git if need be.The GUI is less verbose with the nitty gritty hidden in expandable sections, which makes history easier and cleaner to scroll through, also no scrolling bugs, rich text is easier to read with tables, and images integrated into the chat, resources like browsers in the context of the session. Drag and drop session organization (pins), scheduled tasks, etc.. all that in the side bar.Usually a TUI would be open in VS Code and scoped to whatever repo I'm working with so 10 projects, 10 VS Code instances open, not super scalable. With the GUI desktop app it's one app, and I can start sessions in an repo and switch between them easily, no need to open VS Code for each. I don't see what could make me want to go back to using a TUI.Who else is just using the GUI nowadays, or are you still on the TUI, and why, have you tried the GUI interfaces?

articles.title: GitHub New pull request overview page in public preview
articles.summary: GitHub New pull request overview page in public preview

top_comments: We’ve been building our own Review Pipeline, including automated review guides, risk detection and much more.There’s SO much to be done around Code Review, I’m very surprised GitHub isn’t doing more.They have the reach already, they have years of real review data. And yet, the PR itself is not using any of the newly available methods for more efficient review.Agents are hammering PRs out left and right, and yet here I am still staring at the raw diff of 35 PRs and end up being called the bottleneck.

This is a major improvement and still not great. I made CodeApprove (https://codeapprove.com) 6+ years ago just because the PR page on GitHub is so bad and I felt the urge to make it better.IMO the correct design is pretty simple: - Everything on one page, information dense - Focus on code and unresolved discussions, maybe CI checks - Keyboard navigationGraphite gets pretty close! But it's become cluttered over the years. CodeApprove is far from perfect too (it's been a while since I worked on the UX much) but I'd hope GitHub could do a little better.
I tried it, but I don't understand the fanfare when it's basically the same old UI + a couple of minor layout changes. It definitely doesn't address the needs of the AI dev workflows.
